public_rationale: IDC's October 2024 survey, reported on January 21, 2025, found that 33% of surveyed IT executives cited high adoption costs as a significant barrier, but it did not isolate model-provider prices [e1]. Semafor's January 5, 2024 report described customers choosing alternatives to GPT-4 because of price or speed [e2]. Neither item establishes a deployment blocked by provider prices during January 1–29, 2025, the broad absence of such barriers, or how common they were [e1, e2].
limitations: Both underlying observations predate the target period [e1, e2].
Broad adoption-cost concerns do not identify a deployment blocked by model charges [e1].
The model-selection report does not separate price from speed or establish that deployments were blocked [e2].
A single qualifying counterexample would address the no-company clause but would not establish prevalence.

statement.excerpt: Right now, I do not believe that there are companies that are stymied by the pricing that OpenAI and their ilk offer, nor do I think there are many companies or use cases that don’t exist because Large Language Models are too expensive.

from_speaker: companies that are stymied by the pricing that OpenAI and their ilk offer
nor do I think there are many companies or use cases
because Large Language Models are too expensive
our_interpretation: Treat the belief language as a qualified factual assessment, not a claim about his private mental state.
The ordinary reading is that commercial LLM prices were not blocking companies from deploying otherwise useful applications.
Stymied includes a deployment materially delayed, abandoned or restricted because of model prices; it need not mean the entire company ceased operating.
Use January 1–29, 2025 as the current observation month through publication.
Do not equate integration, training or governance costs with prices charged by model providers.
No numerical meaning is assigned to 'many'.
criteria.support_condition: Contemporary evidence that commercially plausible deployments were not materially blocked by model-provider prices, with sufficiently broad coverage to support the market-level assessment.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A documented company deployment blocked by contemporary model-provider prices contradicts the first clause. Establishing that many companies or use cases were blocked additionally requires evidence of prevalence.

evidence.publisher: IDC research manager Mona Liddell, writing in CIO
evidence.explanation: The survey establishes reported adoption-cost concerns before the post. It neither isolates model-provider pricing nor measures January 2025 decisions.

This is reputable reporting of earlier price-sensitive model selection, used because no underlying customer records were supplied. Switching models is not necessarily a blocked deployment, and the period predates the claim.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Records of January 1–29, 2025 deployment decisions identifying applicable model prices and whether those charges caused delay, abandonment or restricted use. A qualifying example would refute the no-company clause; representative market evidence would be needed to assess the broad absence claim and the separate prevalence clause.
